message.content:
A thin aluminum pan conducts heat rapidly, but it lacks the physical mass to store that energy. Cast iron is dense and heavy. Because a standard cast-iron skillet weighs several times more than a cheap aluminum pan, it holds a vast reservoir of heat energy. This property is thermal mass. 

Consider searing a cold, raw ribeye steak. When the meat hits a thin aluminum pan, the metal instantly loses its heat to the cold steak, dropping the pan’s temperature. The meat boils in its own juices instead of searing. When that same steak hits hot cast iron, the pan’s massive heat reservoir resists this sudden drop. The iron pumps stored energy back into the meat, instantly vaporizing moisture to create a deep, brown crust.

One limitation of this comparison is that it ignores pan thickness. A massive, heavy-duty aluminum baking sheet or a thick-clad aluminum skillet will hold heat much longer than a cheap, paper-thin aluminum pie tin. The weight of the metal matters just as much as the type of metal.
